teaser: Three hunters, a dozen dogs, one small fox. Winter has never been painted colder.

lesson.text: The sky is the color of a frozen pond. No wind, no sun, no shadows. Snow swallows every sound except, perhaps, the crunch of boots and the crackle of one fire. You can almost feel your fingers going numb. Very few paintings give you a temperature this quickly.

Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted it in 1565, in what is now Belgium. The winter that had just ended was one of the hardest of the century there: rivers froze solid and stayed frozen for weeks. Bruegel was not imagining the cold. He and everyone he knew had just lived through it.

Europe was then entering what historians call the Little Ice Age, several centuries of colder winters. Frozen canals became a normal part of life in the Low Countries, and winter scenes with skaters became a local specialty that painters kept producing for a hundred years after Bruegel.

How do you paint cold? Bruegel does it with almost no colors: white, black-brown, and one icy gray-green that he uses twice, for the sky and for the ice, as if one were the mirror of the other. Against that, the men, dogs and trees are dark cutouts. Now, the title promises hunters. So what did they catch?
Three men and a pack of dogs are coming home. Their whole catch is hanging on one man's back. Can you spot it?

spots.title: One thin fox
spots.text: A single fox dangles from the spear over this hunter's shoulder. That is all, for three men and a dozen dogs. The day has been long and poor.

lesson.text: Once you have seen the fox, the whole group changes. The men walk bent forward, and we see none of their faces. The dogs trail behind with their heads and tails down. Nobody at the inn turns to greet them. Bruegel tells you about hunger and tiredness using only backs.
Bruegel made ordinary people the subject of large, ambitious paintings, at a time when that size was normally reserved for saints, kings and ancient heroes.

The picture was one of a set showing the times of the year, ordered by Niclaes Jonghelinck, a rich Antwerp banker, for his country house. There were probably six panels, and five survive. Three hang together in Vienna, including this one, which stands for the deepest part of winter.

It is painted in oil on oak boards, 117 by 162 cm (about 46 by 64 inches). On that fairly modest surface Bruegel fits a hilltop, two villages, a wide valley and a mountain range. The trick is in how he leads your eye from one to the next.
You are standing on a hilltop, just behind the hunters. Follow the route your eye takes into the valley.

lines.label: The hunters' path
lines.text: The dogs, then the three men, each one smaller and farther than the last. They are walking away from you, so you automatically walk with them.

lines.label: The edge of the hill
lines.text: The snowy ridge cuts the picture on a diagonal. Everything on this side is near and large. Beyond it, the ground drops away and the valley opens far below.

lines.label: The way out
lines.text: From the ponds your eye zigzags past the church, across the white fields and up to the sharp peaks. The picture runs for miles.

lesson.text: The four dark tree trunks do a similar job. They stand like posts along a road, each one thinner than the one before, and they measure the distance for you. Bruegel also places you high up, like a bird. This raised view lets him show near and far at once, the hunters at your feet and a whole country beyond them.

Those jagged mountains have nothing to do with Belgium, one of the flattest places in Europe. About twelve years earlier Bruegel had traveled to Italy and crossed the Alps on the way. He drew them, kept the drawings, and went on slipping Alpine peaks into Flemish landscapes for the rest of his life.

So far the picture is about three tired men. But Bruegel was famous for something else: filling a scene with dozens of tiny lives, each busy with its own affairs. Down in the valley, winter is not only hardship. It is also work, and games.

lesson.title: Down in the valley
lesson.text: Leave the hunters on their hill. Three stops below, from the nearest to the farthest.

spots.title: The fire at the inn
spots.text: A family feeds a straw fire outside the inn, probably to singe the bristles off a pig. It is the only warm color in the whole painting, and the flames lean with the wind.

spots.title: A load of sticks
spots.text: A figure crosses the little bridge under a big bundle of firewood. In a winter like this one, keeping the house warm is a daily job.

spots.title: The frozen ponds
spots.text: Dozens of tiny black figures skate, pull each other along, and play games with sticks on the ice. Each is only a few strokes of dark paint, and yet you can tell who is falling.

lesson.text: This is what makes the painting so rich. The same cold that sends the hunters home nearly empty-handed gives the village children a playground. Bruegel does not choose between the two. He simply shows both, from far enough away that no one is the hero.

The banker did not enjoy his paintings for long. In 1566, only a year after they were finished, Jonghelinck offered his art collection, Bruegels included, as a guarantee for a friend's unpaid debt to the city of Antwerp. The pictures later passed to the Habsburg rulers, which is why three of them are in Vienna today.

Bruegel died in 1569, just four years after this winter. He left about forty paintings, and two sons who became painters and copied his inventions for decades. The snowy village seen from above, with skaters and bare trees, became one of the most repeated images in European art. You have seen its descendants on Christmas cards.

spots.title: The crooked sign
spots.text: The inn's sign hangs askew, holding on by one corner. Small signs of neglect like this add to the feeling that times are hard here.

spots.title: The gliding bird
spots.text: A bird hangs in the air with its wings spread, a black shape against the green sky. It marks the empty space between hill and mountains, and makes the drop feel deep.

spots.title: The pack
spots.text: Greyhounds, a red hound, small curly-tailed dogs: no two are alike. Their lowered heads tell the story of the day as clearly as the fox does.

spots.title: The frozen mill
spots.text: Long icicles hang where water should be running under the mill. Its wheel cannot turn, so no grain can be ground here until the thaw.

spots.title: A ride on the ice
spots.text: One figure tows another across the ice on a small sled. A spot of red clothing is enough to catch your eye from across the room.

spots.title: Borrowed mountains
spots.text: Sharp, rocky peaks that Bruegel remembered from his crossing of the Alps, set down behind a Flemish village.

lesson.text: Four centuries later, the Russian director Andrei Tarkovsky put this painting in his science fiction film Solaris. Aboard a space station, a character stares at it for a long time: it stands for Earth, for home. Go back to that green sky and the crunch of snow. A picture of one hard winter in 1565 has become many people's picture of winter itself.

quiz.question: What do the three hunters bring home?
quiz.explanation: One thin fox hangs from a spear on a hunter's back, a poor result for three men and their dogs.

quiz.question: Who ordered the series of paintings this panel belongs to?
quiz.explanation: Niclaes Jonghelinck, a rich banker, wanted the set for his country house.

quiz.question: Why are there Alpine peaks behind a Flemish village?
options: Bruegel had crossed the Alps and reused his memories
quiz.explanation: He drew the Alps on his journey to Italy and kept placing them in his landscapes.

quiz.question: Which color does Bruegel use for both the sky and the ice?
quiz.explanation: The same gray-green appears above and below, so the ponds seem to mirror the sky.

quiz.question: What helps you feel the distance between the hill and the valley?
options: Tree trunks that get thinner one after another
A bright sun low on the horizon
A river that runs straight to the back
quiz.explanation: The four dark trunks shrink step by step and measure the depth for your eye.

facts.text: The painting was made right after one of the harshest winters of the century in the Low Countries.
facts.explanation: Bruegel painted it in 1565, just after a winter when rivers stayed frozen for weeks.

facts.text: Bruegel shows the hunters' proud faces as they return to the village.
facts.explanation: We only see their backs, which is how he conveys their tiredness.

facts.text: The work is painted in oil on oak boards.
facts.explanation: It is an oak panel of about 117 by 162 cm.
